sections.What the paper proposes: The paper (Seasonality in the Cross-Section of Stock Returns) proposes For each stock, the average of its monthly returns at the annual lags 24, 36, 48, and 60 months before the holding month (i.e., the same calendar month as the holding month in each of years 2 through 5 prior) as the signal, sorted by deciles, favoring the highest decile (decile 10, winners) of average returns at annual lags 24, 36, 48, and 60. Rationale: Persistent seasonal variation in expected returns: individual stocks persistently earn different (relatively high or low) returns in specific calendar months, so stocks that did well in a given calendar month in past years tend to do well in that same calendar month again.
sections.What we implemented and changed: We adapted 4 fields and assumed 5. Adapted: breakpoints (no exchange or size breakpoints in our universe; equal-count sorts of eligible names); disfavored_group (policy: long-only, no short leg); universe_and_filters (policy: our 415-name S&P 500 survivor universe); sample_period (policy: our snapshot sample). Assumed: skip_window set to 0 months; price_floor set to none; min_lags set to mean of available lags, at least 2; min_history_days set to 252; min_formation_days set to 15. Portfolios were formed in 131 months with 36.9 names on average.
sections.What the backtest found: Over the sample the strategy returned 8.03% a year net of costs, against 12.71% for the equal-weight universe and 13.45% for SPY. Its Sharpe ratio was 0.38 against 0.65 for the equal-weight universe, and its maximum drawdown was -44.9%. The alpha t-statistic was -1.71; it is reported, not used as a gate. Robustness across costs, sub-periods and ranked groups gave a rho of -0.71.
sections.What the simulation and economics found: Across the simulated paths, incremental fee income versus the equal-weight universe fund had a median present value of -$3.0M, with a 5th to 95th percentile range of -$7.2M to $1.8M. The share of paths with positive NPV after research cost was 12.2%, and 49.5% once the historical excess return is removed. Break-even AUM is not defined; it is reported, not headlined.
